utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-03-69-T, Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The first matter I'd like to address is the suggestion by the Stanisic Defence that would give an opportunity to ask further questions to Dr. Eekhof. The Chamber will take the following approach but is welcoming any further input from the parties. The Chamber would like to receive an updated report before the weekend. The Chamber would also like to receive a report after the weekend. And we want to reschedule the Monday and Tuesday sessions. Now, depending on the circumstances, we could add another day to the weeks after that then sitting three days a week, which would give more time for preparation and, of course, everything depends on how the health situation of Mr. Stanisic develops, but to have lengthy discussions about that at this moment doesn't assist greatly. Another option still would be, although I'm saying it with some hesitation, to move to the Thursday and Friday next week. What we want is not to lose court time and at the same time give fully respect that the rights of Mr. Stanisic should be observed appropriately. And, therefore, we are trying to see whether we can serve both these interests, and of course, the fair trial rights are first, but at the same time we are trying not to lose or rather to -- yes, to lose court time also in the interest of Mr. Stanisic, because no one is served by having this case being dragged along for another additional year. That's the approach we'd like to take. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to apologise for interrupting you, however, it was my impression that you were going to conclude this issue. Hence by your leave, I'd like to address you. We would like to exhibit full co-operation, and we fully understand the attempts made by this Chamber not to lose any court days. However, this represents a difficulty to us. Mr. Petrovic and myself has spent a prolonged period of time here, and we had the June schedule ahead. Since there should have been a break between the 9th and 15th, we had planned to travel to Belgrade in that week. We also received plane tickets from the Registrar, and we wanted to anticipate the further list of witnesses in order to know precisely who would appear at what time so as it to be ready and make things easier for the court. I believe so far we have been rather successful. We had counted on this break, and we scheduled a number of meetings with the witnesses and people we wanted to see who were intended to appear just after the break, rather than to spend time here sitting around waiting to see which day of the week we'll sit next without doing anything that would be of our client's interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So to put matters short, at this moment you would say, rather not move next week to the end of the week because that causes us problems. Second, if we would sit more, don't do it on Monday the 14th or Tuesday the 15th, but rather than, for example, on the 18th, which is the day after the two days for which the case was scheduled, the 16th and 17th of June. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this issue with respect to the witness, the witness, as I said yesterday, is scheduled to travel on Friday. Could I ask, or what the Prosecution is requesting, is that the Chamber ask Dr. Eekhof to provide a report tomorrow and that the Chamber make its best decision on the best information that is available tomorrow and advise the Prosecution whether it wants us to continue to have the witness get on a plane or whether it wishes us to do whatever, but I would appreciate some guidance about whether we should bring the witness or continue to have the witness travel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, our approach would include that the witness wouldn't have to travel. Now, at the same time, the option for the Friday -- the Thursday and Friday, the 10th and 11th of June seems to cause a problem, which would then most likely result in adding another day to the week after that. We have to consider that we didn't have the input of Mr. Bakrac before. So it may well be that the Chamber will decide -- of course, unless tomorrow Dr. Eekhof would tell us that everything has been fine for the last few days, but rather than entering into lengthy debates on medical matters, the Chamber prefers to find solutions which avoid discussions in this field which always have some level of what is possible. What is not possible? Why is four and a half hours a day possible but not five days? Why is two days possible? Is three days possible? But of course, what I'm -- I asked for the input of the parties, part of that would also be that if matters get a bit better and if preparation is still at a level which is acceptable whether Mr. Stanisic then still would prefer to come to the courtroom or to attend the hearings from the videolink. All options, all ways of at the same time paying proper attention to what are medical problems and not to overstep what is possible, and at the same time to see how we could proceed with this case without unnecessarily losing time. That's our purpose. Mr. Bakrac gave his input. I take it that we may receive input from you as well, but most likely, Mr. Groome, there will be no hearing on Monday and Tuesday as matters stand now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So am I free to direct VWS to hold off on travel plans until we hear further from the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but finally, and later today, we'd like to hear from the Stanisic Defence whether they would prefer to see whether we can have two days at the end of next week despite the problems Mr. Bakrac may have with that or whether there would be any objections against three days a week in the weeks after that, which would mean that we catch up and compensate for the two lost days. Where I have to add that it was already in the Chamber's mind to look at it more at the possibility of sitting more than two days a week in the near future.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear later today perhaps from you, and we'll try to resolve the matter in such time that the witness does not travel in vain to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's appreciated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have two witnesses still to be cross-examined. Matters are related. I take it that we'll start with Mr. Strinovic. Yesterday the Defence asked for further time to be able to connect the various documents to each other and to see whether that causes major problems. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There are no major questions -- sorry, there are no major problems. Those that there are can be dealt with in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same goes for Mr. Simatovic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then is my assumption right that we'll start with Mr. Strinovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could Mr. Strinovic be escorted into the courtroom. Any estimate of time, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For the first witness no more than five, ten, minutes. For the second, approximately 20 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I'm concerned, we'll need five to ten minutes for the first witness and 15 to 20 for the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Strinovic. The Defence is now ready to cross-examine you. The first who cross-examines you is Mr. Jordash, but before I invite him to start, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jordash, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have very few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I please ask for Exhibit P00512 to be brought on to e-court. And the page I'm looking for is page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the entry, Mr. Strinovic, I'm going to direct you to is entry 9. And the name of Ivan Zelember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I go to page 9, please, of the exhibit. Sorry, page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We can turn -- can you just have a look at entry 9 there, Mr. Strinovic. Ivan Zelember, and you place the comment in the cause of death or date of disappearance as follows: "Fracture to the right side of the face bone, right upper jaw and also to the left side of the scapula and left arm. Brownish jacket, dark shirt and brown pullover." I suspect you wouldn't be able to do this from memory, so we might have to turn to the autopsy report, but let me just try to see if you can. Can you confirm that there was no evidence of gun-shot wound when you looked at the autopsy report? Would you like me to ask for the autopsy report to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also for the Chamber. We have no access to it so we'd like to have a look at it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: My apologies. Could we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you. Yes, that's right, we are looking at the new autopsy reports with only B/C/S available at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which doesn't make it easy for us to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Strinovic, the best way for you to explain to the Court your comment as we've just looked at the last column of your chart is to explain looking at the autopsy report precisely what you conclude was the cause of death with reference to the report, and if you would read the relevant bits so the Court can follow in the absence of an English translation.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relevant information in this particular document is as you can find it in the English translation, i.e., the injuries recorded in the autopsy report are stated therein. We have no cause of those fractures stated, only the fractures you can find in the English translation as well. Out of that description it is difficult to provide definitive reason or cause of death. There was definitely a trauma which came about be it by the use of a blunt instrument or a projectile or an explosion. That is something I was unable to conclude. That is why you find my conclusion as such in the English translation with the injuries listed. One, there were injuries; two, this was definitely a violent death, however, it is difficult for me to conclude what the cause of those injuries was if I look at this document alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You cannot be sure that the death was caused by any particular mechanism?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to explain next. With cases such as this one where there are fractures without any specific characteristics, for example, on a bone, there could be something that would indicate the means such as a piece of shrapnel, a projectile, or a blow, however in this case we only have the description of the fractures, and based only on that, I cannot draw conclusions on the manner in which such injuries were caused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is there anything in the report which would indicate in any way that this was caused by a gun-shot wound of any kind?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I can recall concerning this document, had something like that existed, I would have mentioned it in the English translation, but looking at this protocol, I don't see such a piece of information that would provide an answer to your question, i.e., the specific manner by which the injuries occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For Your Honours' reference, this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to point out that there is a second page. Maybe the doctor would just review that before we leave the document. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. Could we have the second page on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 2, mention is made of an injury in the area of the left scapula as well as the left upper arm. These are additional injuries which alone cannot tell us anything about the manner of those injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, perhaps it's very practical since we have it on our screen now instead of getting it back on our screen at a later stage. You said this is a violent death, although you do not know whether it's shrapnel or bullet or blows or -- do I understand you well that the picture in its totality excludes then for a simple fall of that person which would have caused those injuries or -- so that it is violent, not falling within the scope of what you would normally find if there is just an accident? I'm not talking about very complex accidents, that's of course, another matter, but a normal people falling or from the stairs or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can confirm that. Given the location of those injuries and fractures, on the head, the chest, as well as the limbs, such as the upper arm, such injuries occur be it by multiple blows with blunt instruments or as a consequence of projectiles or explosions. This does not come about by a mere fall down the stairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I've got nothing further on that point, thank you. And those questions for Your Honours' reference were in reference to paragraph 36 of the indictment. Could I have, please, on the e-court Rule 65 ter 05575. Another autopsy report which is only in B/C/S presently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is an autopsy report relating to Danica Razov, and we can turn, if need be to your chart, but your chart notes as the cause of death, no visible injures, defects on the surface of the stomach and softening of one part of the brain, cause of death, cerebral impact (according to pathologist who performed autopsy, cause of death is listed as freezing). Could you elaborate on that a little, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could you first link this to one of the items in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, yes. Page 29 of P00512. Item 28, Danica Razov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, new autopsy report. Therefore, no translation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Cause of death described by Mr. Strinovic as no visible injuries, defects on the surface of the stomach and softening of one part of the brain described by pathologist as freezing being the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you elaborate a little on that, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just need to describe briefly how death due to freezing is ascertained. The finding is normally quite nonspecific, which means when there is no other cause of death, that is obvious to speak of, no other forensic findings and a person was found somewhere when it was cold be it inside a house or outside where there was a low temperature, then freezing is considered as a possible cause of death. When there is another cause of death that is suggested, as in the case of Razov Danica, there is obviously some cerebral damage there, there is softening on the brain which tells us that was incident, maybe some kind of a stoke that occurred. The brain was left without the appropriate amount of blood for sometime obviously, and this is another possible of cause of death. My opinion would be that this was a natural death, perhaps a kind of stroke that occurred in the brain area. If I'm not being sufficiently clear, please by all means let me know and I can explain more. Nevertheless, my conclusion is natural death, cerebral haemorrhage or stroke, which is or more less the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Again for Your Honours' reference that's paragraph 32 of the indictment. I've got no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. Do I understand that it's difficult now than if someone had a stroke to determine whether due to the circumstances in which that person suffered a stroke finally the person died of freezing or whether that person died and then ended up, due to the circumstances, in a situation where the body was frozen; is that how I have to understand your explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this case we are looking at a person who was obviously not in good health, she was 67 years old at the time of her death. The postmortem showed that there were changes to the brain in those sections of the brain where the damage caused would lead to immediate death. These are vital sections of the brain. When there's a lesion or damage that occurs, death follows immediately as a result. After death, the person may have happened to be in a cold place, and therefore, appearing to be frozen, but the true cause of death in this case was irreversible damage to a vital section of the person's brain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you disagree with the cause of death as described in the report, and you would say on the basis of the findings it may have been cold but that's not what the person died of. Thank you. This finishes your cross-examination, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, do you have any questions for Mr. Strinovic? Mr. Strinovic, Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic, and he will be the next one to cross-examine you, and perhaps I explain to you that I could call you Professor or call you doctor, with due respect for all your qualifications, I have the habit of addressing all witnesses by Mr. or Ms. or Mrs., and this is not in any way expressing any disrespect for you -- for your academic qualifications. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Professor. His Honour Judge Orie has introduced me. I only have a handful of general questions for you, sir. If my understanding is correct, that the findings of the PMs that occurred at these various locations, would I be right in stating that there were only two locations, specifically Skabrnja and Nadin where you were working with, what shall I call them, fresh bodies, persons who had been killed two or three days before the PM took place? And all the other postmortems did not take place until much later, three, five, or six years later in some cases?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when talking about the bodies from Skabrnja and Nadin, I would like to have the following played in e-court. This is Prosecution Exhibit 65 ter number 4634. Starting at 1 minute 20 seconds, or rather, 1 hour 20 seconds, 41 minutes then up to 1 hour 23 minutes, 30 seconds, please. That is the section that I would like to upload.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take that it's not the kind of video of which the Chamber yesterday said it would not assist its understanding of the case. There must be something not just illustration but something that clarifies a matter which is in dispute, is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. At this point in time I don't see a witness that we could use for this exhibit, to tender this exhibit through. This witness appears to be our best opportunity. The document shows who was in charge of handing over the bodies on this occasion. I would merely like the witness to tell us whether what the video reflects is consistent with his own knowledge of what happened and how the bodies of those killed were retrieved. I think this might be helpful to you as far as locations themselves are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about how and by whom the bodies were handed over? Could you -- perhaps we first ask the questions to the witness and then see whether there's any dispute because as you may have become aware of, the Chamber is not assisted by looking at some unidentified or even identified autopsy room or by looking at what the colour was of the -- in which the doctors were dressed when performing the -- or to see a body which is not identified where apparently there's no specific problem with that person. So I hope that the message was clear enough. I think it was for the Prosecution, but it should be for the Defence as well. So let's first -- if you first perhaps ask the questions to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus was on her feet, I should give her an opportunity to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was just merely to inform the Chamber that this video is not in sanction, so it would take -- if the Chamber would like the video to be played, it would take the Case Manager a few minutes to be able to manage it technically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll first see whether there is any need to look at the video which will not be elicited by just asking questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour. Perhaps you are right. I will try to take this up with the professor and try to deal with the matter in a simplest possible way by following your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Professor, do you know that the bodies of the people killed on the 18th and 19th of December, 1991 -- November, I'm sorry, I actually said December in Skabrnja and Nadin were taken or brought there by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know who performed the postmortem on those bodies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Forensic pathologist from Zadar, Dr. Dujlan [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about the pathologist you mentioned, did he perhaps tell you that the JNA allowed him to inspect the bodies since the JNA was at the time holding the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't actually know that for a fact, but I assume that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, could you please try to put your questions in a non-composite manner because is it true that they were brought there by the JNA is too different matters. First of all, that there were not there yet but were brought there. The second question is by whom were they brought there. With the last question, it's the same, did he tell you that the JNA allowed him to inspect the bodies since the JNA was at the time holding the bodies. These are two different matters. You can give permission for something you are not holding, and the second is, whether you are holding those bodies. So let's try to keep focused and avoid whatever way of confusion or mixing up matters. Perhaps we could ask the witness what is the basis for his assumption. You said, I don't actually know that for fact, but I assume that to be the case. First of all, did you refer to the JNA holding the bodies, or did you refer to the JNA allowing the forensic pathologist to inspect the bodies, which of the two, or both elements of the question you were addressing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I said, I'm not familiar with the details. I only found out later on. I received detailed information relating to this case when I first arrived in The Hague, for my first testimony here. I don't know who handed over the bodies or in whose possession the bodies were, I just know the PM was performed in a hospital in Zadar. I know that it was performed by Dr. Ivo Dujlan. I'm also familiar with the findings of those PMs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would not like to take up any more time with this, and I think the Professor's answer was crystal clear. I would like to, therefore, invite the OTP just in case they have nothing else to challenge and as long as they agree that the video-clip shows clearly that 35 bodies were brought there by a JNA truck and also the military persons are mentioned there who did the hand-over, if that is not something they wish to challenge in that case I would like to move for the 65 ter exhibit to be moved into evidence. There's no need to go through it to have a look. We have the Professor's answer. I'm not sure if there's anything else here for the OTP to challenge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the transportation of the dead bodies a matter which is in dispute? If it's unclear or if you do not know, then, of course, it's a possible matter in dispute and then we'd have to look at it because Mr. Bakrac tells us that the video supports his view where the view of the Prosecution is still unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I have a moment to consult?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's something we would like to check into with your leave, before we respond. We didn't know that the Defence was going to show this document -- this video, so we'd like to look into it. We'll do it as soon as we possibly can, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then if it's unclear if we would have to return later because this would be the last part of your cross-examination, Mr. Bakrac? Or would there be more?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. No, no, it's not the last question. I have two or three left, general ones, Your Honours, if I may. As far as this is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the difference with the matter yesterday is that I have not seen anything on that video what reasonably was one could consider to be in dispute. Here it seems that at least a matter of potential substance is shown and under those circumstances, I would like to allow Mr. Bakrac to play the video. Mr. Bakrac, you may play the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Laugel is prepared to play the video now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The booth has received no transcript of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, there's no transcript available. Have you provided it to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. My mistake. Quite simply, I had not announced this exhibit. It's part of the 92 ter package of the OTP. Therefore, I assumed that there was a translation available, as has been the case with all documents up to now. I do have the transcript in B/C/S. The number is 65 ter 4634.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there's no translation. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the transcript is in e-court, if Mr. Bakrac identifies where in the transcript -- it hasn't been provided to the booth because the booth didn't know that the Defence was going to play it, so normally we would provide a transcript in advance to the booth, so perhaps either it can be brought to them and/or it could be somehow shown on the screen or something. Called up in e-court. It's in there under that 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that you resolve this matter during the -- no, we are not yet at a break. How much more is it, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have the transcript in e-court, but I know that the booths are not able to see it. I'm not sure if it might be helpful to perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long is it? The transcript -- the portion of the transcript you would like to use? Is that one page or ten pages, or?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three pages -- four pages, Your Honour. No, again, correction, four and a half pages in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that they will be printed out, they will be distributed to the booth and that we then look at the video. That may take awhile. At the same time part of what I said yesterday is that we got a lot of explanations from persons on the screen. There it was one of the witnesses who had told us already three or four times the same. Here it is an unidentified person. Mr. Bakrac, if he is going to tell you that orange car is a JNA car, then, of course, then it really goes to the substance, and I don't know whether this is the way in which we want to receive that evidence because wearing a -- I would say the doctor's clothes doesn't make him immediately as an expert. But I don't know what that followed, and apparently the Prosecution also doesn't know. But I want to keep matters clean. Ms. Marcus, do you know who this is and what --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. Just very briefly, a number of general questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, Professor, we have so far agreed that these were the only two locations, Skabrnja and Nadin, where you conducted autopsies with bodies that were still relatively fresh, so to speak. The remaining bodies were bodies that were beginning to mummify at this stage already, you've said that, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Professor, would there be any changes to the clothes in terms of decay over a three-to-five-year period? Would rot begin to set in? Would the clothing get even more deformed, so to speak, over the three-to-five-year period?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as any changes that occur over time to bodies as well as clothes, this can vary to quite a high degree, and the changes can vary in nature. Sometimes the bodies and the clothes will decay faster and sometimes they will be preserved for a longer time, even over five years. Although, of course, you can tell that there was damage to the clothing. The colour pales, but the relatives may be able to identify a specific piece of clothing even after ten years. Nevertheless, any damage that occurs is clearly visible, such as tears, for example, or bullet-holes, shrapnel, anything like that. Quite often even after the three-to-five-year period we can still find damage to the clothing that is consistent with mechanical damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: During your examinations and the autopsies you carried out, have you ever come across a situation whereby you found damage to the clothes which would not be indicative of the mechanism and manner of the creation of those injuries?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Clothes are no primary indication of the manner injuries are caused. It can only serve as an aid. If we have injuries, if we have something that we believe is suspicious, then the clothes can be used to confirm or exclude our hypothesis. However, there are numerous cases where clothes are so damaged that we can determine nothing from it. Such clothes are of no use to indicate anything, let alone any types of injuries. However, we also come across preserved clothes which would clearly indicate or confirm our hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. In situations when there is no more soft tissue and when you need to make conclusions based on bone damage alone, is there a possibility that such damage or injuries occurred due to a single piece of shrapnel which would then resemble a bullet damage or something of that sort?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've stated already, we have cases in which shrapnel can actually resemble a bullet, i.e. of the same velocity and appearance resulting damage that would be quite similar and difficult to differentiate. Such damage to the clothes and on the bones can be very much alike or even identical. This primarily is seen in cases of high velocity projectiles, for example, to the skull occurring at high velocity and causing damage which we cannot with any degree of certainty ascertain the cause of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Ms. Marcus, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, simply the remaining question of the exhibits that were marked for identification, the chart and the underlying documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll ask the Defence first -- because we had several types of objections. utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, I do understand that the Prosecution and the Registry are preparing a -- kind of a new structure in which the material related to the testimony of Mr. Strinovic and of Ms. Bilic will be put in a kind of a geographical order but then being put together that each location receives one exhibit number and that the beginning of that exhibit, which then consists of several documents, would be an index of what exactly how many, and which previously 65 ter numbers are to be found in -- under that one exhibit number. utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's acceptable of course. The one question, just for clarification, does that mean that the underlying documents for Dr. Strinovic that were on the 65 ter list are then admitted into evidence with the chart and the new documents being marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's better to wait at this moment. Why? Because for the chart we do not know whether any inconsistencies are found once Mr. Jordash has seen the translations. And we all are aware that Mr. Jordash's reservation is exclusively in relation to not yet translated underlying documents and the way in which they are reflected or presented in the chart. Let's try to keep matters simple. And the parties all understand, I think, where we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, this concludes your evidence in this case. I'd like to thank you very much both for answering all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, but also for your patience and the homework you had done in dealing with all the charts and giving your comments on it. You are excused, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be preferable to start now with the cross-examination of Ms. Bilic? Most likely both parties would not conclude it or to have an early break and then try to do it in one session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We would prefer an early break because we are trying to sort out something which would make the cross-examination quicker. So we would go for that option. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I may take it that there's no objection from the Prosecution to that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break and we resume at five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, welcome in the court room. If you would forgive me, I would just briefly address a practical matter with the parties. One of -- Mr. Bakrac, I'm asking you specifically. utterances.text: And you would arrive in the morning so that we could start in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. Unless there is another volcano erupting somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take care of that. There will be no eruptions until that day. Yes, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the request of the Stanisic Defence is that we not sit next week because even, in our submission, if Mr. Stanisic would recover or have some kind of recovery tomorrow by Friday, we would still be in a position not to have had ample time to take the instructions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what is the problem if we are talking about the 15th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would leave the whole of the week open if we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We would support that request, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: First, can I ask for Exhibit P516 to be brought on to the screen. I just want to refer you to the chart where you entered comments concerning authenticity and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, I'd forgotten to introduce Mr. Jordash to you. He is counsel for Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The entry I'm interested in for the moment is number 1 concerning Missing person Ernest Baca, and you note on the right-hand column that the missing persons report indicates that this person went missing in mid-September of 1991 in Kotlina in Baranja. On the column to the left of that, you note that this was a case where there were two questionnaires for the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For completeness sake, could I now stand to -- could we have 65 ter 0187 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This, I'm going to suggest, is the second questionnaire. If you just have a look at that, please. Please let me know when you've had an opportunity to read that.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go to the second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just, could you bear this in mind, that I am going to ask you to confirm that this second questionnaire relating to Ernest Baca suggests that somebody is saw Ernest Baca in 1992 in a Serb camp in Jagodinjak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must confess that I don't see where it is stated that he had been seen in a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps we need to go to the next page because I don't see it on page 2 either. Can we go to page 3. And also the -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's in paragraph 21, item 21 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the fourth page in English. At least that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't get it, is everything what we see in English visible now in the B/C/S version for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, except we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see 39/91 and then a bit of text follows under 21, but perhaps I have not the full picture of what the witness sees. 21, there's an asterisk, and the asterisk takes us down to 29 in the original. Let me see what happens there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to 29 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently not all of the text which appears under 21 is there in the original, or am I wrong -- because under 29 a reference is there to an asterisk takes us to 29, but in 29 it's about which, if any, list article beginning 1992 and that seems not to be exactly the same as.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah, there does seem to be some discrepancy which I hadn't observed before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So what now appears under item 21 seems at least the second part, a woman witness allegedly saw him somewhere in October 1992, seems not to be there in the original. Perhaps somewhere else, but certainly not in 21. So perhaps you take your time to find it somewhere in the document, it may well be that it's somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps I can leave this point until a little later and ask a member of our Defence to check that while I move on to another point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me take you back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on e-court, please, P516 again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr is going to help you out, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, I was just going to mention that it is on ERN page 0103-6717 of the B/C/S, which is page 5 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there it appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Given the confusion that existed a moment ago, can you confirm that that is the -- the B/C/S says in relation to entry 21, probably at the Beli Manastir police station under the questionnaire states 30th of the -- let me cut that short. Does it say in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the problem is that the original appears on two different pages. A woman witness apparently is on page 6717 last four digits original, whereas the other entry is found under paragraph 21 in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps I can try and shortcut it. Madam, does the B/C/S from what you've seen under 21 and the notes at the end of the form, suggest that a witness had seen Ernest Baca in 1992 in a Serb camp in Jagodinjak?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the answer provided to item 21 it is stated that Ernest Baca was positively seen in front of the police station in Beli Manastir. There is also an additional note at the back of the page that there was a witness who stated that she allegedly saw him in a Serb camp in Jagodinjak in October 1992. It seems that there was a positive identification in front of the police station in Beli Manastir, and the alleged seeing of the person in the Serb camp in Jagodinjak as stated in the request for a search for this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How are you able to choose one above the other in terms of adopting one identification and not the other?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We accepted the date of disappearance, which was specified by the person requesting that the person be found, which seems to be positive, and we discarded the alleged spotting of the witness whose identity is not even specified in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But on what basis did you discard that second identification? What made you conclude you could not rely upon it such that you could rely upon the first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first try to understand what we are doing at this moment. This is a person apparently missing, yes. Now, apparently the issue is whether he is still missing. That may be of your major concern, whether he is found or not, whether he is located so that his family knows where he is. Is that what it's all about, Ms. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As far as I understand, the counsel wanted to know what criteria we used to ascertain the date of disappearance in September 1991 instead of going for the date of disappearance in October 1992. We chose the date of disappearance based on the degree of certainty of the person submitting the request for search of Ernest Baca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On the other hand, you said a moment ago that the person who made the second identification wasn't identified on the form, so how were you able to ascertain that witness as a certainty?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I'd like to clarify something. This comment on the back of the page, which is not part of the form, was something provided by the person initiating the request for search who as the date of disappearance specified September 1991. However, that person was obviously in contact with some other witnesses whereby he or she learned that the missing Ernest Baca was allegedly seen in 1992 and was still alive at the time. So we had the same source of information. Both dates, that is, come from the same source, the source being the person initiating the request. If we were able to see the whole questionnaire, it would be clear. It will become clear that the second piece of information about Ernest Baca being seen in 1992 was provided by the same person as an additional piece of information arrived at by himself which may contribute to the search itself. If I can add something, I would say something in answer to His Honour's question. Mr. Ernest Baca was identified later on. His mortal remains were found in the Republic of Serbia. He was handed over to Croatian authorities and positively identified on the 12th of February, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps it's me but I'm not quite following. If we can -- the person who identified Mr. Baca as going missing in September 1991 was the same person who identified him in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to work out. I'm not following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to understand. What is apparently registered here is that most probably he has been seen for the last time on the 30th of September, 1991 in Beli Manastir, and that he has not been seen since then apart from this same person telling when he was seen for the last time also referring to an unnamed source who would have told the reporting person that that unnamed source thinks that he has seen him in a camp in 1992, whereas, finally the bodily remains were found and were identified. That's how I understand your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I still have problems in understanding how -- is it your suggestion that you would say on the basis of an unnamed source who saw him once that then that's the date on which he disappeared? I mean, if the facts are known, then whether you choose for the one or the other, the story is apparently as the witness told us someone reporting, we saw him for the last time, but we once heard from another person that he most likely had seen him at another place. I mean, then you have the full story.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If the person who made the identification on the second occasion was right or might have been right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is then -- then he was still missing since 1991 but at a certain moment was spotted by someone at another place, which doesn't invalidate the first observation that from Beli Manastir he had not been seen again and that -- I do not see the real point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The real point is that paragraph 37 of the indictment puts this witness as a victim of Arkan who shot him along with 25 other Croat detainees. So in October of 1991, according to the Prosecution, he was dead, and according to this witness he might have been still alive in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what we'll have to do is we will have to compare the data from the autopsy, where the body was found, when the body was found, whether we have any further details there and then compare that with the unnamed source and see what is true or not. It's not -- it's comparing the two stories rather than to say what is the date of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: All I was seeking to do was ascertain whether the second report had been properly considered by the expert witness and properly dismissed. If it hadn't been, there might have been a doubt that that witness was a victim and that might prove important in the end in terms of an eventual sentence. I was simply seeing if there was a doubt and raising it if it existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You very much attach it to the date of disappearance, whereas, I looked at it as this is what we know as a story from disappearing, some doubts as to whether he was still alive at a certain moment, and we have the autopsy report, and we have to carefully consider whether the one contradicts the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the autopsy report, I mean, I don't have it in front of me, but in terms of this point, whether the unfortunate man ended up dead, doesn't necessarily change the situation if the unnamed witness who saw him or purportedly saw him was accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on what we find in the autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Exactly, but it may not actually touch on the subject that I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do not know that, but now it's clear to me and if you want to stress the importance of comparing all the information we have before we reach any conclusions, then the point is perfectly clear. Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just going to note for the record that on the authentication chart of Mr. Strinovic, it indicates that no autopsy report -- and again this is a new untranslated report 65 ter number 5540 indicates that the autopsy was performed in 1991 in Novi Sad Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't seen that yet, but that's of course the problem with all the new reports which have not been translated and which we cannot read, although perhaps it wouldn't be bad to have a look at it perhaps later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I take Mr. Farr's word. I know he is fluent. So I take his word for that, and I can move on. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have it on the screen while you are continuing so that we can have a look at it. Could we have 65 ter 5540. Unless you have any further questions for the witness in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Not on this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could we -- if you would please proceed and meanwhile we can have a look at P5540.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: It's on page 5, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify, my comment was based on what we find in Dr. Strinovic's chart rather than in the underlying document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. At the same time, that should be reflected in the document, isn't it? But we are interrupting you again and again, Mr. Jordash, which we shouldn't do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to do, Ms. Bilic, the same exercise with the missing person Josip Balog. Please could we have P516 on e-court at page 8 and it's entry 2. P516. Page 8, please. Entry 2. And I see there your entry under authenticity and a reference to two questionnaires and your conclusion that Mr. Balog went missing on the 28th of September 1991 in Knezevi Vinogradi.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I please have Rule 65 ter 00160 on e-court. That's 00160. Sorry, I think I've got the wrong one, I do apologise. 65 ter 03054 is the missing persons form I want to refer to. That's 03054. And can we turn to page -- just have a quick look at page 1 just to confirm what it is. And can we go to the next page of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And once you've had an opportunity to look at that, can we go to page 2. Are you ready for page 2?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2, please. Can we go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps while that's happening, if I can read you what I'm interested in from page 2. It may be that you remember this. It says under the title "information of the forcible" -- oh, we are there. It appears to indicate that in the second report concerning Josip Balog that the date and hour of the disappearance or the date of his becoming missing, the 20th of November 1991 at 7.30 a.m. from Vukovar. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this before. Nevertheless, what we are looking at here is two entirely different persons. One person is Josip Balog, who went missing, I'm not sure when but I think it was August or September 1991 in Baranja. What we are looking at here is an altogether different man also named Josip Balog, which is obvious if you look at his date of birth. This is a person who went missing in Vukovar. The only thing the two share is their name, but these are, in actual fact, two different persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for the answer. Can I move to methodology now, please. You testified yesterday about your role in compiling the missing persons form. Could you explain the process by which it was compiled, when I say compiled, I mean designed. Are you able to provide some detail as to how it was designed?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can try. First and foremost, standarised forms were used to compile information on missing persons. First of all, the ICRC form followed by the United Nations Human Rights Centre and the INTERPOL form used to officially publish that a person was missing and a search would then be launched. Having gathered all these materials, a Working Group was put together including people from the Ministry of Internal Affairs, people from the forensic institute and criminal medicine, members of our office for missing persons and prisoners of war headed by the president of that office. The general form was agreed that would be used and it was to be based on the existing standard forms. Nevertheless, it was also agreed that the form would need to adapt to the peculiarities of the situation that prevailed in Croatia itself. Each member of the Working Group was in charge of a section of the questionnaire that they were then to design and prepare, a special set of questions, each within their own remit. The proposals were then forwarded to the committee of Croatia's government for missing persons and prisoners of war. The methodology used was then adapted to the sets of questions in order to be able to process all the information electronically and to avoid gathering too much descriptive information. Despite this, the objective was to have a sufficient amount of detail as to enable us to better try and track down these missing persons. This is the procedure that was used to compile this form on missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. The objective was to have a sufficient amount of detail to enable you to try and track down any missing person or missing persons of a Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose for putting together this questionnaire was gather information on any missing persons who went missing as a result of the war. The public campaign was launched for that reason as well, so first the form or questionnaire was compiled and this was followed by a public campaign calling on all the families of missing nationals of the Republic of Croatia to start a procedure in order to try and track their relatives down. And this applied to any case which in one way or another had to do with the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So there was no thought at that stage that this was going to be predominantly designed to assist finding Croats as opposed to other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to try and find any persons who went missing amid the armed conflicts regardless of their background, ethnicity, religion, or indeed any other distinguishing factor. The fact is during this operation, a lot of information was gathered and information was gathered as well in relation to ethnic Serbs who went missing during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask for 65 ter 03054 to be put back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This form, which we looked at a moment ago, is identical to the form that was designed; is this correct? This is typical of the forms?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This would be a typical sample of the form that was used to collect information on missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to the top of page 2, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, is this typical B, information on formation affiliation. 18, the missing person was at the moment of the forcible taking-away/disappearance/capture, a member of (a), HV Croatian army active forces; (b), HV reserve forces, and so on down to (g), other defenders of RH? Is that typical of the missing forms?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the questions that was always there and used in the forms that we used during the 1994 campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There isn't -- or is there, a space designed for other ethnic groups? Is that a fair reading of 18?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information that was asked under item 18 was about the status of the missing person and not the missing person's ethnicity. It was about the status. At the time of disappearance, a person was either a member of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia or alternatively a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about members of the Serbian forces at the time the person disappeared? Why isn't that on the form?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the whole campaign was launched in 1994 in a bid to track down any missing persons, there were parts of Croatia that were still occupied. Back then, there weren't in actual fact too many such cases occurring where families of missing soldiers fighting on the other side, on the enemy side, so to say, were submitting requests for searches to be conducted. Nevertheless, we did encounter a number of cases where families would add, for example, that they had a relative who was a JNA member or a relative doing their regular military term of duty in the JNA at the time. And that is as much as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let's leave aside the reality on the ground as to who was or wasn't going missing. What I'm interested in is the format of the form. The questions that the form was asking and the form appears to ask only in relation to Croats. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Jordash's previous questions were related to question 18. As he has now phrased the question, I think it misstates the information that is on the form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has answered to some extent the question that is about status. I think -- I don't think you would disagree with me, Mr. Jordash, that what you are actually asking the witness is why there are no non-Croat organisations mentioned here in this question of which the witness said was aiming at establishing the status, was the status as being a soldier in the JNA or in the SRK or in BiH Army, was that not relevant for you, that apparently is the issue you want to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, put it much clearer than I did, but yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you comment on what now appears to be the question of Mr. Jordash, why only Croatian institutions and, may I take it that MUP active forces refer to Croatian MUP active forces, it doesn't say so, but why there is no reference to any organisations, structures, which are beyond the Croatian organisational structure? Why no question was he a JNA member? Why no question was he Republika Srpska Krajina army member? Or whether why he was -- whether he was a BiH, HVO, whatever, everything which does not appear here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's put it this way: The form was compiled in 1994. This was three years after the outbreak of war in the Republic of Croatia. As I said at the time, parts of Croatia's territory was still occupied. It would not have been realistic to expect that any considerable number of families, of members of paramilitary units would now address the authorities or specifically our office for missing persons and prisoners with requests for searches to be conducted, although, as I said, there were such cases where families would write in to say that some of their relatives were members of the JNA, JNA reservists, or doing their military term in the JNA and the like. Beyond that, it is also noteworthy that the form was compiled in order to gather information on missing nationals of the Republic of Croatia. We, as a commission, were in charge of gathering information and compiling records concerning missing Croatian nationals and not missing Serbian nationals or indeed missing BH nationals. The reason being simply, these countries had their own bodies that were in charge of similar searches and procedures which had been set up precisely for that purpose, and it was these bodies that were in charge of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask, please, that we move to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I'm interested towards the bottom of the page number 8. The question there, who carried out the forcible taking-away/capture of the person, and the list of possibilities underneath, was that typical of the form?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a typical question in this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there room on the form or a question which was designed to deal with missing persons who had not been forcibly taken away or captured, or was it a presumption of the form that the missing persons would have been forcibly taken away or captured?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not the presumption in the form that each and every missing person was forcibly taken away or detained. However, this question made its way into the form in case that there had been detention or a forcible take-away, and if the person initiating the search had information about the persons or units that carried out this forcible take-away, such information should be forwarded. If there was no such information, if the person went missing, say, in action, for the most part, answers were not provided to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, just for me to understand, the form again and again repeats the three categories that is forcible taking-away, disappearance, capture. Now, thinking about these three options, when I'm thinking about a question who did it, that is a relevant question for taking away and for capture, but for disappearance, it seems logically but perhaps it's my understanding of what these words mean, someone disappears, who did it, no, he disappeared, so therefore, with the whole of the form again and again has the three categories, would you agree with me that for the type of question we find under the heading you just addressed, that it would be a useless question for those who just disappeared?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How was paramilitary units defined in the minds of those who compiled the form? What was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first invite Mr. Jordash to finish his question. If you have any objection then we'll hear from you, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was the definition that was agreed, if any, by those who compiled the form when considering question 8? I managed to keep Mr. Farr on his seat.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for any members of paramilitary units or units themselves, it was understood that it should include members of the armed forces active in the territory of Croatia that was occupied. In other words, it wasn't the JNA. It had to do with local population which fought against the republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go back, please, to page 2. And back to 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: (G), other defenders of RH. Am I correct that there was a presumption that the forces within, or the Croatia forces, I should say, were defenders as opposed to perhaps a more pejorative term paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to -- for me to speak about this part since I'm not familiar with any military structures and the laws regulating this issue. Hence, I don't feel competent to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But you worked with the forms for many years. The subject of other defenders of RH must have come up at some point. What was your understanding of what that term did in terms of defining the Croatian forces? And I intentionally compare that with paramilitaries when referencing those fighting Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, I'm not sufficiently familiar with the system of the military. I can only speak from memory as to what was specified under this item. Still, I don't feel adequately equipped to answer this question. I don't even know what the legislative framework regulating this issue is even nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me then that the process of compiling missing persons of Croat ethnicity avoided defining any of them as paramilitaries but defined them as one form of defender or another; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, perhaps a very practical question: If someone would report that the missing person was a member of a paramilitary unit, would you then fill in the name of that unit under 18(g)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We would not have entered it under 18(g).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you then tell us, give us an example of what you would enter under 18(g)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, a member of the HOS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: HOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think it is short for the Croatian defensive forces although I'm not positive about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me turn, if I can now, please, to your report. P514.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have that on the screen. And can we go, please, to page 31 of the English and page 13 of the B/C/S. It should be -- I'm looking for Number 30, data on missing persons, so I might have given the wrong page, but it's 30, and it's page 30 of -- page 30 of the English, 30 is also the section, and the B/C/S should be page 13, or perhaps 12 for the beginning of the section. Now, this is the section which deals with data on missing persons and dealing with the administration for detainees and missing persons and the resolution of 1.976 cases and the outstanding search request for 1.076. I know the figures have slightly changed, and I'm not concerned with the figures directly, but the definition. So can we move to page 31 of the English and the paragraph which starts "of the 1.076 missing persons" reference to the attachment. "In terms of gender, 860 are male and 260 female; in terms of the status, the fate is unknown of 542 civilians, 98 members of civilian protection, 402 Croatian defenders while the status of 34 missing persons is unknown." And that's in reference to the figures which are below where the Croats are the majority. Are you following me so far?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, with reference to this figure where the Croats are the majority, how was it that civilians were defined precisely? Was this something that came directly from the families or those reporting the missing person?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All information in this part of the report concerning ethnicity, gender, age, as well as the status of those missing is based on the information provided by those initiating requests. That is to say, members of their families much as was the case with the form provided by the international committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there any standardised definition of civilians which was applied to the description given by those making the requests?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There probably was. I cannot recall it off the cuff, but these would be persons not belonging to any armed forces, and who did not take part in any defensive tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who didn't at the point of going missing or never had or, I mean perhaps I'm asking you to speculate since you've just said you cannot recall it, but, I don't wish you to speculate.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know precisely, but I can only presume that these were persons not belonging to any armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What would be in your mind having worked with these forms, the difference between say civilian protection and paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of civilian protection carried out their regular duties and tasks such as utility tasks, things that had to do with shelters, et cetera. This was the basic task of civilian protection, as opposed to defenders who were members of the armed forces and as well as opposed to civilians who did not have such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What if a civilian protector carried a gun at times during some of their duties, would they still remain civilian protectors, or would they become something else in the minds of those compiling the reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has indicated that she doesn't really know exactly how these categories were determined. I think that at this point this is asking for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, she reviewed them and she filled them in now and then, therefore, if the witness can give an answer, she is invited to do so. If you can't, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In such a case, the person would probably have been registered as a member of the armed forces, in the example you used, if there was a member of civilian protection who used weapons. However, it is only a presumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the term Croatian defender be used to describe all organised military formations of Croat ethnicity from the Croatian Armed Forces to paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian defenders were not only Croats. Their ranks included people of all ethnicities, however, the term Croatian defenders is something that was used for those belonging to the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia. I have to reiterate yet again though that I'm not familiar with any military structures, especially in terms of legislation which defines and regulates the status of Croatian defenders. Therefore, it is very difficult for me to provide a detailed and precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about military structures, I'm asking you about the definitions that were used in compiling information, and that's in your report. I appreciate you are not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 32, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, this is with reference to data compiled in the period from 2002 to 2006 and 874 missing persons where the majority this time are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I'm interested in the sentence which says: "In terms of status (according to statements by their family members) 401 were civilians, 428 persons were members of military formations, where the status of 45 missing persons is unknown." First question is this: When we looked at the previous page, there was no caveat expressed when the majority of missing persons were Croats, that the information was, according to statements by their family members. Is there a significance as to why it's there when the majority of missing are Serbs? Perhaps I can simplify the question. Was there a skepticism about what was reported by Serbian families concerning civilian status?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. There was no skepticism whatsoever. In both cases the data is based on the information provided by family members and those who initiated search requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But only in relation to when the Serbs were the majority, and we'll come -- there's another entry which is exactly the same. Only when the Serbs are the majority is there this caveat according to statements by their family members, which might be read as expressing a degree of skepticism. Do you know why that caveat is there in relation to when the Serbs are the majority missing but not when the Croats are missing and are in the majority? Perhaps so it's clear, I'm referring also to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all background noise please cease.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm also referring to page 34 which relates to the exhumation -- well, we'll turn to that in a minute. Was there a significance in that statement, or it has no significance according to you?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was absolutely no skepticism concerning the status specified.
