I wanted to add something else, as for the status of those exhumed, although we still not have arrive at that part one could discuss the issue of caution. If it was formulated the same way concerning those identified. It had to do with the following: The status of those identified from the first group, that is to say, the 3.100 of them, even if the person was allegedly a Croatian defender that could be checked against the official records. Depending on that, there were further procedures concerning internment. In the cases where the family stated in the case of those 380 persons missing, when the family stated that the person in question belonged to a military formation, we had no way of verifying that piece of information in any of our records because such information was simply not available to us. What it was, I believe, was a degree of caution in question, trying to provide as clear an explanation as possible about the way we obtained that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But in relation to -- sorry, which official records could you check to see if the Croat was a member of -- or could be termed a Croatian defender?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said already, the source of information about a status of those missing, which is the basis of the information put in the report, is based on the statements of their family members. However, when we are discussing those identified, in such a case, if the person in question was a Croatian defender, his or her status was ascertained with the administration in charge of the issue of Croatian defenders. This was a department in the ministry I worked for. In that regard, it was important to ascertain the status of those identified, because according to the law on the rights of war veterans in Croatia, Croatian defenders enjoyed different rights, or rather, their families had some additional rights what had to do with funerals. It was for that reason that for each person identified, a check was carried out to confirm the late person's actual status of a Croatian defender.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you able to check the status of the 1.881 persons identified as civilians?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those people were civilians, and they are not in the records pertaining to Croatian defenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That was the definition that was used to corroborate the initial request, that they didn't appear in the records of the Croatian defenders?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I have to say I did not understand this comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, may I try to assist you. What Mr. Jordash is putting to you is that someone who is not registered as a member of a regular or at least, administrated armed force, is not necessarily a civilian because if someone without being registered as a member of the army or the police or nevertheless takes up weapons for the purposes of what we are discussing here, they may be considered not to be civilians because they are carrying arms. Now, that apparently is something what Mr. Jordash is addressing, Mr. Jordash, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what Mr. Jordash now wants to know is whether there's any chance that someone who you could not identify as being registered as, well, let's say as a soldier or member of the armed forces, that you would more or less automatically put them on your list as a civilian, whereas Mr. Jordash says, well, even if not registered, if armed, they might not have been civilians in this context. Mr. Jordash, did I understand the issue well, and could we ask the witness to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Could you please comment on what I just explained to you and which is similar to what Mr. Jordash did put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best. There were individual cases where I don't think anyone could rule out the possibility that a person carrying weapons was classified as a civilian. Nevertheless, there could have been no more than individual cases of this happening. There was no default classifying of persons as Croatian defenders or civilians. This could not have been the case and, in fact, was not the case. Most persons who were indeed Croatian defenders were also recorded as Croatian defenders and their records were kept, also because under the law on Croatian defenders, their rights and the rights of their families, their families enjoyed certain status related rights. In most cases, if not all, these families obtained all of their entitlements eventually. So this could only have occurred on an individual basis, on a sporadic basis. But as long as we are talking about the official records, we must lend those some credence. On the other hand, it's very hard for me to say anything about possible individual cases or the status of these cases at the time when a person went missing or was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You cannot comment on the completeness of these Croatian defender records, can you? You can only presume because certain rights would attach to becoming registered that everybody or most people would have done so; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said this was one of the reasons. But this certainly wasn't the way in which the records of Croatian defenders were created. It was certainly not the way in which these records or the database was created. The database was created based on the official records of the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Internal Affairs concerning members of the armed forces who were involved in the defence of the Republic of Croatia. That is how the database was produced, and this was an official database. Could there have been individual cases where something else happened or not? Well, that's very hard for me to say from where I stand, but the database was official and complete and was being used and still is used, as a matter of fact, in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How do you know it was complete? I accept it was official, but how do you know it was complete?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The database was created by unifying all the databases of the relevant ministries of the Republic of Croatia whose members were also -- or employees were also members of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the point you apparently want to make is clear, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's of course 100 per cent completeness, well, I would not put my money on that. On any database. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go to page 34, please. And I'm nearly finished on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And please would be you able to explain page 34 and page, I think, 13 or 14. Yes, page 14 of the B/C/S, and I'm looking at the paragraph besides mass and individual graves. Perhaps we can go up the page, please, to the top of the B/C/S page and bring the English page down a bit. I just want to read something and ask for your comment. "Besides mass and individual graves, the remains of 700 persons were exhumed in the Republic of Croatia who were buried in common graves following the humane terrain restoration of mortal remains from the Storm military-police action." I think we've got a glitch in the system. Sorry, our system is playing up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your last words appear again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. We need to go to the next page, I think of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, the bottom paragraph there, Ms. Bilic. "Besides mass and individual graves, the remains of 700 persons were exhumed in the Republic of Croatia who were buried in common graves following the humane terrain restoration of mortal remains from the Storm military-police action." Maybe I'm not reading this correctly or maybe I am. So what is the reference to the humane terrain restoration?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I try to answer that question, if I may, I would like to address your comment in relation to the previous question. You said you weren't sure that any database, even an official one could ever be complete. That was precisely what I was trying to say when I said that individual cases were possible in which the database was not complete, but on the whole and generally speaking, the database was complete. As for the humane terrain restoration or the humane evacuation of bodily remains of those killed, the bodies were gathered in a relatively broad area. Each of the bodies was recorded and then they would be buried in graves that were prepared already and in keeping with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to your comment about the record and the completeness of the record, did the record record any paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I just would ask Mr. Jordash to perhaps specify exactly which records he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier questions were put about paramilitary groups. An example of what was filled in was given HOS. Now, I don't where exactly to draw all the lines in the Croatian system, still to be explored. Could you be as precise as possible, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the question was a general one because I was seeking to explore for Your Honours whether those records were complete in another sense, in the sense of what was recorded as well as who was recorded as a member of the military formation. So the question was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps in order to avoid whatever confusion, Ms. Bilic, several times the expression "paramilitary force" or "paramilitary units" were used. Are you familiar with that concept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In answering to one of the previous questions, I said what was implied by that expression, paramilitary formations. The expression denotes members of the armed forces from a part of Croatia's occupied territory who were rebels and who were waging war on the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be quite a bit of confusion. Apparently you consider the armed forces of -- the armed forces which were operational in areas of Croatia which were occupied, at least not under Croatian administrative control and military control. You consider that to be paramilitary forces; is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part, yes. But those weren't just paramilitary formations, there was also the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. But for example, the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, you consider that to be a paramilitary force; is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, going back to what on those parts of the -- see on the Croatian force apart from the example we just discussed, are you aware of any paramilitary forces other than the one we've mentioned either Croat paramilitary forces or Serb paramilitary forces or Bosnian military forces. Could you give us an example of any other paramilitary force operating on Croatian territory whether occupied or not, and not being the armed forces of what you called rebel forces or the rebel government. Could you give us any other example of paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Regrettably this is not a subject that I've been studying, and I don't think I'm qualified to address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whether you are qualified or not, is -- if you know anything, if you say, well, my neighbour told me that the ABC forces are paramilitary forces, or I saw a newspaper article about the paramilitary forces by the name of XQY, then whether you are qualified or not, I'd like to hear from you. If you have any idea, any impression for yourself of what you understood to be paramilitary forces not being the type of forces I just mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really have no other information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I explored this because I felt that there may be a total lack of understanding on what you are talking about and what you are asking the witness about and that her perception may be a totally different one from yours. So please keep that in mind when you continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I may be jumping the gun, but I've only got two or three more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two or three more questions. And then for after the break, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, after the break I have some questions which I cannot fit into the remaining time before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I do understand that. But you can fit it into the remaining time after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I certainly hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And hopefully even in such a time that Mr. Jordash, his 10 to 15 minutes which he asked for yesterday would also still remain. Mr. Jordash, your last three or four questions, you said two or three, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just going back to your definitions of paramilitary formations. That's a term that those involved in, the compilation of these records understood as applicable to Serb forces or forces fighting the Croatian forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the term "defender" was understood by those compiling this information to apply to Croatian forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what that meant was that those who were not Croatians reporting missing persons must have been to a degree regarded by those compiling the data as coming from the aggressor forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've been saying, the question was not envisaged in the form, was a missing person a member of a paramilitary formation. There was, however, the option if the person's family wanted to address the issue when submitting a request for a search to be conducted to clearly say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you would still suggest that this compilation of data of missing persons was an impartial exercise, would you assert that, nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Compilation of data and missing persons from the first appeal to the general public and then down to the last steps that were taken in relation to each individual missing person was always following the same procedure regardless of a person's ethnicity, religion, or any other type of affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've got no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. We first have a break and we resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good evening, Ms. Bilic.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have several questions for you. First of all, I would like to briefly go back to the form for missing persons, 65 ter 3054 you were looking at a awhile ago, question number 18. Shall we have that on our screens again, or do you know what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can check in my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case can we please have that displayed, 3054 page 2, question 18. 3054 page 2. Question 18 in the English copy, it's in the next page. Could we please have the next page, which may then be page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, question 18, you say that you were directly involved in filling one of these forms; right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question to you is how would you fill in the form on behalf of a national of the Republic of Croatia who is a member of the Serbian Army of Krajina whose family wishes to submit to you a request for missing persons? How would you fill in the form as regards question 18, please?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would simply supplement the question. What I would like to say is this question is no obstacle at all to submitting a request to conduct a search by Serb families, even in cases in which their missing relatives were members of armed paramilitary formations. The fact remains that as this sort of information was gathered, searches were launched in relation to 131 ethnic Serbs. There were some members of the armed forces among them as well. Other than that, between 2002 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, can you please restrict yourself to answering my question which indeed you have done. So you would supplement the question by adding information to it; right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many cases like that occurred in which information was added to the form? Did you come across a single such occurrence where the form was added to by saying that a missing person was a Croatian national who was also a member of the Army of Serbian Krajina? How many cases can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember a single case where that type of information was stated. The person being a member of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I can remember cases involving members of the JNA or JNA reservists though.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So we have a person who is a Croatian national and a member of the paramilitary formations of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, so-called the Republic of Serbian Krajina but that's hardly of any importance whatsoever. No such cases were, in fact, recorded of such a person submitting a request and succeeding in getting the form through to your office; right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I'm saying is I can't remember any cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. What about Croatian nationals who were members of paramilitary formations in the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina? Was there another procedure that they were allowed to follow, I mean their families, in terms of reporting their absence of those persons going missing?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those relatives would report their own family members going missing to the relevant bodies in the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could they have reported their absence of them going missing even if the families were in the Republic of Serbia, could they have, for example, reported the person going missing to the Red Cross, International Red Cross, the Red Cross of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree, of course -- you will agree with me that there were cases like that, quite many, in fact, at the time we are talking about, 1991 prior to Operation Flash and Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you right now is about our administration for missing persons and prisoners of war. There were 131 requests submitted by Serbs, ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But that's not what I'm asking you, Ms. Bilic. I'm asking you if you know whether there existed quite many forms and questionnaires in relation to missing persons who were Croatian nationals submitted to the International Red Cross be it in Belgrade or field offices in other countries of the former Yugoslavia and further afield, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. This information was then taken up by the ICRC, right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the ICRC and the relevant commission on behalf of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have access to ICRC information regarding missing persons? Such information as was available between 1991 and 1995 prior to Operation Flash and Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have access to that information. There was a joint database, as a matter of fact, and this was published all together in the book of missing persons published by the ICRC in co-operation with administration for missing persons and prisoners of war and the Croatian Red Cross. All of this information was put together at the same time by the ICRC and the administration for missing persons and prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, in your report, paragraph 30 specifically, it is mentioned that there was a request to launch searches in relation to 3.052 missing persons. What about this figure, 3.052 missing person? Does this represent the total of the requests submitted to the ICRC in relation to Croatian nationals who were members of paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this information was not part of the overall figure. It wasn't included in the overall figure. Instead it was published in the book of missing persons in the territory of the Republic of Serbia. The figure that we are looking at 3052 search requests is actually in relation to the search requests that were collected during the campaign back in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, first of all, why the information was not included or covered by the this total of 3052 persons who were Croatian nationals going missing during the war in 1992 and certainly before Operation Flash and Operation Storm, why is that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we are looking at two different campaigns of collecting information. During the first, forms were compiled for these 3.052 persons. And in the other campaign, it's difficult to say now, but I think it was about 1.200 persons in the other campaign. At the time the report was drawn up, it was 1.110. During the other campaign that was launched, a relatively small number of family member reported persons who went missing, and these were families who had not previously filed a report with the administration for missing person and prisoners of war whose family members had gone missing at some point prior to Operation Flash and Operation Storm, however, we were dealing with a relatively small number of cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's only now that the interpreters have finished the English translation. Could I ask you to make a small pause between question and answer. Mr. Petrovic will show you how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, in 1994 and 1995, the information that was available to you or made available to you by the ICRC was not taken into consideration when the total number of those missing Croatian nationals who went missing, why was that not taken into account? I'm not talking about the list that was drawn up in 2002, I'm talking about what I specified.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, at the time the information was not included because it was not available to the administration on missing persons and prisoners of war in that form. The criteria for distinction were not sufficiently clear at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Ms. Bilic, my question is why, why was that the number not covered by the total? Can you answer?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can offer no more than I've said. Information in relation to 3.052 persons is about the requests that were filed during the 1994 campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then what about the other lists that we are talking about that? That wasn't drawn up before the period between 2002 and 2006, right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please tell us -- can you please tell us this: What about the territory of the Republic of Croatian -- what about the territory that was actually under the control of Croatia's government, how many people went missing in that territory? Between 1991 and Operation Flash and Operation Storm, how many people went missing in that part of the territory?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say right now. Not with any degree of accuracy. I know that in Gospic seven persons were reported as missing, in the [indiscernible] 19, nevertheless it would be very difficult for me to address the question of the total number of missing persons throughout that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, why were no records kept then of people who went missing in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, that part of the territory that was actually under the control of the government between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is simply not true that no records were kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: My objection was that he was misstating her evidence but she has corrected it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue and complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not true that no records were kept of the missing persons in the territory under the Croatian authorities. Records were, in fact, kept, but I can't say off the bat what the exact figure might be. I had not expected this question to come up, and I have not updated my information on that. Nevertheless, regardless of the place where these persons went missing anywhere at all in the Republic of Croatia, records were drawn up in relation to that as long as their families submitted search requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a special database or files relating to the persons, the category of persons that I'm addressing at the time I specified, anything that you know about?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't a special record or a special database. There is a unified, a joint database for all missing persons who went missing during the war in the Republic of Croatia, nevertheless, the agency allows us to update our information according to all the required criteria, therefore, the criteria that you had just specified could be used to update that kind of information and obtain an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To sum up, Ms. Bilic, you or anyone in your office, in fact, never tried to update this sort of information based on the following criteria, people who went missing between 1991 and 1995 during the war in the territory that was actually under the Croatian authorities and control by the government of the Republic of Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, all the information is being constantly updated, and the only thing that really is true is I am unable to say at this point in time what the figure is of the persons who went missing during that time in the territory that was actually under the control of Croatia's government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please slow down. I mean, I have to switch from one booth to another to see how far they are behind, and that's not their mistake, that's your mistake. I am not blaming you, Ms. Bilic, but Mr. Petrovic knows what he is expected to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to the interpreters primarily. I apologise to you, Your Honours, as well, and particularly to the interpreters because of the speed of my questions, however, I have to keep in mind the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, what about the list in relation to the other category of persons, persons who were in the territory controlled by the Republic of Serbian Krajina and persons who were members of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and who went missing following Operation Flash and Operation Storm? The list first began to be drawn up back in 2002, right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that was back in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, why did it take seven years for such a vital list to begin to be drawn up, vital for the families of those persons who went missing, what took so long?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, for the most part the families of those missing persons were at the time staying in the Republic of Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. For the most part those families were not physically residing in the Republic of Croatia. Other than that, families would launch these procedures primarily with the ICRC. Some of the families would report their own relatives who went missing to a number of NGOs active in the Republic of Serbia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I do have to admit that there were certain disagreements as to who was in charge of keeping records of missing persons during Operation Flash and Operation Storm. There was also some dispute about the methodology that was to be used in terms of gathering information on those missing persons. Negotiations were held in 2000 in Zagreb, more specifically in July 2000, where an agreement was reached with the relevant commission in charge of missing persons of the government of the Republic of Serbia. The agreement concerned launching or taking some steps to start gathering information, based on the same methodology and the same criteria as the one that had occurred in 1994. Following that, there was a series of working meetings, people were trained to take these steps and to take these measures and the operation finally began in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, what kept Croatia's government from doing this for a full seven years? I'm not asking you about the specifics of this agreement, but what about the Republic of Croatia? It was able -- the government was able to do something like this in 1994, yet, now it took them another seven years to start doing the same thing in 2002. I realise that there were problems, and I accept that, but this was a vital issue, and it simple brooked no long deferral --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, your question contains some six, seven or eight propositions. Mr. Farr, apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Farr, then I take it that you withdraw your intension to object. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your report, paragraph 15, you provided some definitions, such as the definition of a mass grave and the definition of a communal grave. What about the territory of the Republic of Croatia outside the Republic of Serbian Krajina, were there any mass graves in those areas?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to try and answer the question about why the Croatian authorities took seven years to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question has been withdrawn and, therefore, we don't need to hear an answer on that. There may be good reason, there may not be good reasons, it's not very relevant anyhow. Please proceed. So could you -- when I say, "please proceed," could you answer the question. Were there any mass graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As far as I can remember, there was a mass grave that was identified at [indiscernible] not far from Gospic. There was another mass grave that was found in a part of Gospic known as Obradovic Varos. At this point in time, frankly, I'm unable to remember any other mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, are you familiar with the grave at Pakracka Poljana?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that grave too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a complex issue. As for Pakracka Poljana, the remains of a total of 19 persons were buried. These were bodies that, as far as I am aware, had been found on the ground and buried by the Argentine battalion of the UN operating in the area. The fact remains that the location of the grave was not marked. The fact also remains that the UN Argentine battalion who were the people, who buried those bodies, recorded the finding of those bodies and the marks were found on the actual bodies when the bodies were later exhumed in 1995. It is beyond dispute that we are talking about a place where bodies were buried, in fact, bodies belonging to 19 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, in paragraph 21 of your report, you state that between September 1995 and July 2008, there were 143 mass graves exhumed as well as 1.200 individual graves. Out of this total, how many had to do with mass graves and individual graves of those who disappeared after the military-police Operations Flash and Storm?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean those found after those operations? They all were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't sufficiently precise. Out of this total, in how many graves were there any remains found of those who perished during or at the time of Operations Storm and Flash, out of the number you mentioned in paragraph 21?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortal remains of people who perished in the military-police operations of Operation Storm and Flash were exhumed from communal graves in Knin, Gracac, Zitnic, Korenica, Petrinja, and Dvor so far. As I've said, these are communal graves, and as such, they did not find their way on to the list of 143 mass graves. As for the individual graves, I truly don't know what was the number of individual graves containing the remains of those who perished during the two operations, but it may be that there are between 20 and 30 such locations so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, the grave, or rather, the four graves in Knin after the operations of Flash and Storm, were those graves communal or mass graves, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were categorised as communal graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, if I told you that in those graves in two different locations there were 295 bodies complete bodies found as well as 94 partial bodies without any identification, what would that tell you? Would you say it was a communal or a mass grave in your understanding of the two categories?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Petrovic is giving evidence. If he wants to pose a hypothetical to Ms. Bilic, if a grave was found with certain characteristics, how would you characterise that, that would be fine, but here he is assuming matters not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now, first of all that is not prohibited in cross-examination, to suggest facts which have not yet been established. Apart from that, the question Mr. Petrovic did put comes down to what conclusions would you draw and whether that's a hypothetical situation or a situation which really exists. If it's not established the Chamber will consider it as not to exist and although it may be wiser for Mr. Petrovic not even to suggest the existence of that without any evidence, that Chamber will not misunderstand him. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic, or perhaps we could ask you what would that tell you? Would you say it was communal or a mass grave in your understanding of the two categories, and it's about -- if you would find 295 bodies complete and 94 partial bodily remains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the terms of communal and mass graves, one first and foremost needs to consider the circumstances under which those bodies were buried. As far as I know, the mortal remains in Knin were marked. Concerning the mortal remains in Knin during the sanitation and hygiene measures operation, complete documentation was drafted with a view to carry out a preliminary identification of the mortal remains. Such documents were presented to the families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic. Is there any chance that you would finish in the next couple of minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if it's a matter of a couple of minutes, then unfortunately the answer is no. It was not what I expected. I keep receiving extensive answers, and I am unable to comply. I do believe I still have a number of relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answers you receive are not unrelated to the questions you are putting to the witness. Just to give you an example, I wouldn't say that whether you call a grave a mass grave or communal grave has no relevance at all, but of course, the core of the issue is who were buried there, how did they die, who is responsible for that, how did it happen under the circumstances, and if you would focus on that rather than on a rather theoretical debate on how exactly whether these 19 persons, whether you should call the grave a communal grave and then to go through all the details, which would make the distinction, that's really not the core of what this case is about. Would you please keep that in mind and finish as quickly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm doing my best, but I believe it is clear that I'm putting these questions to try and indicate the degree of credibility -- I apologise, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not a debating club, we are a court floor. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour, I apologise yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, you mentioned that in the Knin cemetery there were markings indicating that certain people were buried there. My question is this: If this was so, if it was known that there were graves there, do you know why the exhumations began only six years later in 2001?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why the exhumations took place six years after the burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will try to do away with as many questions as possible. Another thing that had to do with the procedure of preparation, you said that the people who carried out those activities in 1995 and 2001 were trained to do so, and that they entered information into the questionnaires. Can you tell us why it was so? Why was it done by trained personnel and not those who were in search of their family members?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was precisely because such people needed precise instruction on how to fill out the questionnaires so as to have as quality and detailed answers as possible. If you look at certain questions, especially the anti-mortem data and health information, that is a complex issue, and it does require a certain amount of instructions in order to arrive at answers which would be as precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please bear with me. I have just another topic to cover. Do you have any data on those who were detained in the territory of Croatia under the control of the Croatian government? Do you have such information?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration for detained and missing persons as well as the commission, it functioned before its inception, were not competent to keep records about those who were in the territory that was controlled by the Croatian government in relation to any war time activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did your commission take part in the release and exchange of persons detained on either side?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission did take part in it according to the regulations stipulating its remit. It was one of its tasks to carry out exchanges and repatriation of detained persons. The other task was to monitor the conditions of detention, but it was not its task to keep records of persons in relation to war time activities who were in the territory controlled by the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So there were no records kept --

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say there weren't any records kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to jump up and interrupt my learned friend, but I wanted to alert the Court, I thought it was fair to alert the Court to the issue relating to B-1244. I will not require the 15 minutes, I will only require five minutes having changed our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few other matters as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, any chance that you would finish in the next five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my utmost to comply, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that there were no records kept. I said that this was not within the remit of the administration for the detained and missing persons and the commission which existed before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you were a member of the commission which, as you said a moment ago, was tasked with monitoring the conditions of detention in the territory controlled by the Croatian government. Can you tell us where those people were detained?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persons under the control of the Croatian government were kept in jails and detention centres as well as in centres for prisoners of war and penitentiary institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which locations specifically are these? Can you enumerate as many as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, the penitentiaries of Lepoglava and Pozega. The centres for POWs that was in Lora as well as Sibenika, I think. I think there was one at Koningsknecht [phoen] as well. Concerning jails, there was one in Zagreb, another one in Osijek. Perhaps Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is enough, thank you. Your office supervised the conditions in Lora. What were the results of your monitoring, what information did you have about detention conditions in Lora?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only speak of the information I received after 1993 because that is when I was employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, with all due respect, you should be able to speak of the activities of your office as far back as 1991. Why would you be in no position to address the earlier period before your employment?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I have no information before that. I was familiar with the proceedings in the Lora case only through the media, therefore, I only have very scant information about the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have dropped a number of my questions, and in spite of that, I believe I hope I have met your expectations in terms of time. Thank you, Ms. Bilic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic, you have even left some time which was suggested to you as being available. Any re-examination, Mr. Farr?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I do have a few questions, Your Honour. I'm conscious that our time is very limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could I first have 65 ter 466 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, do you recognise this document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a standard form of the questionnaire with information about those detained and missing. In this particular case the person in question is Anna Tepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can I have the middle of page 5 in B/C/S and the middle of page 4 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I'm interested in questions 12 to 14. Ms. Bilic, based on questions 12 to 14, can you tell us what the citizenship, nationality, and religion of this missing person is?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The citizenship was that of the Republic of Croatia, nationality was Serbian and religion Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In your evidence today, you mentioned -- I'm done with that document, thank you. In your evidence today you mentioned information gathered during the process of creating the common graves following the "asanacija" process, information regarding the people who were buried. Can you tell us what that information was?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: During the process of burying people in the common graves following the "asanacija" process, you mentioned that certain information was gathered about the people who were buried in those common graves. Can you tell us what some of that information was?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information had to do with the place where the mortal remains were found, the time when they were found, the mortal remains were photographed, and a description of the clothes and other characteristics was noted down, which would help in subsequent identification of those mortal remains. If possible, finger-prints were taken as well as a further attempt to identify the mortal remains in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did your administration receive that information?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Upon receipt, it forwarded it to the competent commission of the Republic of Serbia and the competent body for missing persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina where the families of those who perished resided so as to contribute further to their preliminary identification. In addition to that, the information was also made publicly and daily available on the administration premises so that people could have access to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And as close as you can remember, in what month and year did your administration forward that information to the competent commission of the Republic of Serbia and the competent body for missing persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to remember that. I think it was perhaps one year after the military-police operations of Flash and Storm were concluded, although, I'm not positive about that. All information was collated, put into standard forms, and handed over to the competent commissions of the neighbouring states.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender P516, which was marked for identification yesterday. That's the authentication chart with Ms. Bilic's comments on it, and I would also correct to 76, the number of underlying documents identified on that chart. Your Honour admitted 81 underlying documents based on my calculation error yesterday at page 5577 of the transcript. In fact, the correct number of underlying documents is 76.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that we have decided that they would be admitted without numbers already. P516, that -- any objections against P516? If not, P516 is admitted into evidence and the others they'll find their way in the lists and charts, and it is clear that nothing opposes admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Petrovic. I take it that this concluded your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Ms. Bilic, in answer to my learned friend's question, you explained the way sanitation and hygiene measures were taken and how the communal graves were treated. Does this also include the four graves in the Knin cemetery, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This includes the mortal remains buried and exhumed at the Knin cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Since the Judges have no questions for you, Ms. Bilic, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming in and the patience you have shown to us and patience apart from of course answering all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the bench. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, five minutes, and think about my reputation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The application is to -- it's in relation to B-1244, and Your Honours' request that we agree a set of facts summarising this witness's bad character. What I would like to propose and ask Your Honours to allow is, in fact, a new response by the Defence to the original motion. And the reason for that request is that having looked at our response, I do not think we address the evidence in sufficient detail to assist Your Honours. Secondly, in relation to the bad character evidence as indicated in the informal e-mail to your Legal Officer, the documents, which we have to look through number in excess of 280, so there is much about this witness's -- and all of that is not strictly relevant to his bad character, but there is lots of it which is. In our submission, Your Honours, would be assisted in the decision if we were to revisit this issue in light of that voluminous evidence of bad character and relate it to the witness's specific evidence to try to demonstrate to Your Honours why it would not be safe to go down the Rule 92 quater route. At the moment, Your Honours, in our submission on the basis of our response, which is inadequate, and on the basis of the voluminous character evidence which we have to yet to go through, do not, in our submission, have the requisite assistance from the Defence. If Your Honours are not with us on that, we would ask for more time to summarise the agreed evidence because there's, as I've said, plenty of it and we would require more than the week which we initially asked for. That's the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. You'll understand the Chamber would first like to hear the response of the Prosecution if it can be given right away then, of course, we'll have to consider and think about it. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's position would be if the Chamber feels it would be assisted by a renewed response, the Prosecution would not objection to the Stanisic Defence as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any position taken by the Simatovic Defence in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Jordash spoke on behalf of both Defence teams. We discussed this during the last break. Our position is identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will consider it and will give a decision in due course. I have very few and procedural matters. The first one is the following: On the 25th of May, the Chamber has invited the Simatovic Defence to peruse the Croatian crime base of the facts submitted for agreement by the Prosecution on the 16th of February 2010 within a week's time. Since witnesses Strinovic and Bilic testify about this crime base, they have testified, the Prosecution had indicated that if there was no agreement it would seek to tender such documents. Now, the first question would be, has the Prosecution tendered everything from the Croatian crime base that was included in the agreed facts motion of the 16th of February?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We have, Your Honours. The only thing I would add to that is that you will note on reviewing the authentication charts that in some cases where we still did not have any documentation we wrote that we would request that documentation if necessary, but they are very few, if Your Honours would like us to count exactly how many, we'll be happy to do that, but it is a very small number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so I would say most of the -- in this respect quite a bit of the 16th of February, 2010 motion is moot now. To the extent that it's not moot, because that's -- it's there now, so for the remainder, is there -- no, let me just -- yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it certainly may be moot from the Prosecution's point of view with respect to tendering evidence, but certainly if there's an agreement, it certainly saves the Chamber with respect to the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that is -- I was not very precise. It's past 7.00. Is there any chance that on the remaining issues and on the issues which were now supported by all the evidence tendered that an agreement can be reached, or?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether you know, but in keeping with your order of the 25th of May, on the 31st of May, we informed our colleagues from the Prosecution of our position. Concerning Annex A, we identified clearly what is not in dispute in our view, and I believe we encompassed most of what we are discussing here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the Chamber is not informed about this yet, is that correct, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we received an e-mail from the Simatovic Defence, that's correct. In that they say that they agreed to the annexes but they didn't say that they agreed to the facts, so what we took that to mean -- our understanding was that they did not agree to the date of death, the location, the manner of death, et cetera, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do the following. You sit together with the Simatovic Defence and you make a joint filing on what is agreed upon and what is not agreed upon and whether it's -- and then the Chamber will know where we stand. Then one -- yes. The medical journal article which was 65 ter 5183, the Chamber has deferred its decision on the -- this document in its decision on the 14th motion for leave to amend its 65 ter list. We left it out, and we have invited the OTP to elaborate on its intended use and whether it would be intended pursuant to Rule 94 bis. Now we raised the matter on the 27th of May, and then we heard that the Prosecution would consider how to tender the document, whether through expert witness Dr. Strinovic or otherwise. Mr. Strinovic has now given his evidence, this document was not introduced through him. What is the other way you intend to introduce this in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, it was decided that it couldn't be tendered through Dr. Strinovic. With your leave, I'd like to consult with my colleagues and report back to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'd like to hear from you within seven days from today. Even if that will be informal, because the Chamber has decided that -- first of all, Madam Registrar, the Chamber would very much like to receive the next report, as I said, before the weekend, but in order for scheduling purposes, it would important for us to receive that document by tomorrow noon, so if Dr. Eekhof would be able to again examine Mr. Stanisic and then briefly report on that, even if it's not yet officially filed that we know it. Mr. Groome, everything tends now in the direction of not sitting on Monday and Tuesday. The only thing is tomorrow at noon we'll have the last report. If that changes dramatically the situation, we'll consider otherwise, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask Your Honour, it wasn't clear to me earlier, are we sitting on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that once we have -- but we are aiming at this moment at sitting on the 15th, but before we make any final determinations, but what we discussed is the most likely course that we'll take. It also depends on many others who have to contribute to make it possible. We were considering it and exploring it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again my apologies for all those who I hardly can see behind the smoked glass. We'll adjourn for the day, and we'll resume most likely Tuesday the 15th of June quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th of June, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.06 p.m.
